endorsements.quote: A practical implementation approach begins with the formation of an interdisciplinary AI governance committee that includes nurse executives, nursing informatics leaders, frontline nurses, physicians, quality and safety personnel, information technology specialists, data scientists, and compliance representatives.
Organizations should also implement a standardized AI intake and review process.
Before organization-wide implementation, AI tools should be tested in limited clinical environments to evaluate usability, workflow integration, user acceptance, and safety outcomes.

Proposed AI technologies should undergo risk tiring, assessment of clinical usefulness, workflow analysis, bias evaluation, privacy and security review, and validation of evidence supporting their intended use.
Higher-risk applications may require more extensive pilot testing and governance review before deployment.

After deployment, governance committees should conduct ongoing monitoring using predefined performance indicators, including adoption rates, clinical outcomes, workflow impact, safety events, fairness metrics, and user feedback.
Formal reassessment processes should be established to guide model updates, retraining, replacement, or retirement when performance standards are no longer met.

Governance mechanisms should, therefore, require bias assessment before deployment and ongoing evaluation across demographic variables such as race, ethnicity, language, socioeconomic status, disability, and geography.
Accountability structures should define roles and responsibilities for monitoring system performance, approving updates, and responding to adverse events.
Security risk assessments, vendor due diligence, and cybersecurity safeguards should be integrated into AI procurement and lifecycle management processes.

Before go-live and during updates, health systems should assess the type and intensity of education required for each AI-enabled application and develop interprofessional training plans that combine didactic instruction, skills validation, orientation content, and ongoing competency review.
For nursing governance, transparency includes clear communication about when AI is being used, how recommendations are generated, and what role human clinicians retain in final decision making.
Patients must understand how their data are used, particularly when AI models rely on secondary data analysis or external vendor partnerships.

unlisted_practices: Embed nursing professional governance representation, such as shared membership or joint committee participation, in AI governance bodies.
Involve direct care nurses in AI vendor evaluation, workflow design, testing, validation, and postimplementation optimization.
Define guardrails for human review, escalation pathways, and safeguards against automation bias so AI augments rather than replaces clinical judgment.

screen.reason: This is a framework and perspective article outlining a system-level AI governance model and recommendations for nurse leaders rather than an empirical study.
